sections.html:
Mississippi State University defines this market. The school was founded in 1878 as the state's land-grant college, and it changed Starkville from a farm town into a college town. The city is the Oktibbeha County seat in east-central Mississippi and the biggest city in the Golden Triangle, with 24,360 people at the 2020 census. The county overall had 51,427.

Median age here was 28.7, and 40.8 percent of households were one person living alone. Buyers, renters and the school year all pull on a sale. Countywide, the median owner-occupied value is $171,500, and 49 percent of households own their homes, so roughly half of all housing is rented.

sections.h2: Timing a sale around the semester
sections.html:
Location decides who sees your house. Near campus, the audience is students, parents, faculty and investors. Farther out, it is mostly families and university staff. Owner-held homes were vacant far less often than rentals in 2020, which tells you that the landlord with a house empty between leases is usually the one under the most time pressure.

  • A lease ending in May or August makes a clean handoff possible, or leaves a vacant house running up bills.
  • With tenants in place at closing, the buyer cares about the lease terms, so collect the lease and rent records early.
  • A house needing work between tenants often sells more smoothly to an as-is buyer than to a financed retail buyer.

Decide early whether you want to show the house occupied or empty, and let that choice set your target closing date.

U.S. 82 bypasses the city along its north side, running about 25 miles east to Columbus, and Mississippi Highways 12 and 25 also come through. Twenty-two Starkville sites are on the National Register of Historic Places, so if your house is an older one near downtown, ask early whether it carries a historic designation. A buyer will want to know before any exterior work.

sections.h2: The Cotton District and walkable neighborhoods
sections.html: The Cotton District, begun in 1969 as a New Urbanist neighborhood near downtown, is a compact, walkable area with thousands of residential units and many restaurants and bars. Houses and units there sell on a different logic than a suburban three-bedroom: investors look at rent potential and student demand, while families look at yard size and school zoning. If you own there, expect questions about leases, parking and noise. If you own farther out, lean on space, quiet and commute.

When heirs share a Starkville house, sales slow down over small things: who has authority to sign, whether taxes were paid, and where the deed was recorded. Settle those first. Then gather repair receipts, tax bills and any lease, and decide together whether to list, sell to an investor or accept a cash offer. An as-is buyer can close without anyone in the family spending money on repairs.

The county does both the valuing and the collecting. February 1 is the due date for the prior assessment year. Both the Tax Assessor and the Collector work from 101 East Main Street in Starkville, and 662-323-1273 reaches them.

The Mississippi Constitution sets two ratios here. A single-family home its owner occupies falls in Class I and is taxed on 10 percent of true value. Other real property, including a house rented to students, is Class II at 15 percent. Combine the county, city and school district millage and apply it to the assessed value to reach the bill.

Landlords feel the difference most. Their rental pays on a larger share of value, and a house that stops being owner-occupied can lose its homestead credit. Real property is revalued at least every four years. To dispute a value, go to the Board of Supervisors, normally by the first Monday in August.

Taxes left unpaid can lead to a tax sale. State rules permit sales on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August, and the county Tax Collector can tell you what applies to your parcel.

The exemption belongs to whoever lives in the house on January 1, so it does not pass to a buyer. A new owner files at the Tax Assessor's office between January 1 and April 1, and qualifies only by owning and occupying the house as a primary residence on January 1 with the deed on file at the Chancery Clerk before January 7.

Owners younger than 65 receive a credit of up to $300. Owners 65 or older, or totally disabled, are exempt on the first $7,500 of assessed value, and some disabled service members and surviving spouses are fully exempt.

None of this helps an investor who buys a Starkville rental, because it will not be a primary residence. A family buying a first home early in the year may wait until the following year for the credit, which is worth mentioning when you negotiate.

Under Mississippi Code section 89-1-503 the seller hands the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement ahead of the title transfer. A buyer who gets it after making an offer can pull out in writing, within three days if it was handed over or five if it was mailed.

A Starkville owner has three main paths. A retail listing can work well near campus when the house is in good order and the timing suits the academic year. A sale to another investor fits a rental with tenants. An as-is sale straight to a cash buyer avoids repairs, showings and lender conditions.

A house that has stayed in a family for years deserves a close look at old deeds, unrecorded transfers and shared heirs while the title search is under way.

Start any sale with a title search. An attorney or title company will find unpaid taxes, mortgages and liens, then prepare the deed. The Chancery Clerk records it, and it needs a notarized seller signature and a legal description. Bring photo identification, tax receipts, any mortgage payoff figure, and lease copies if tenants live in the house.

After you sign, balances owed are paid from your proceeds and the rest goes to you. In a cash sale there is no buyer's lender, so the stages that wait on a loan approval do not apply.

Cash Home Buyers talks with Starkville sellers about as-is sales, including houses with tenants or deferred repairs. We lay out what we can do and when, so you can compare it with listing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Starkville rental house with tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer takes the house subject to the existing lease, so you provide the lease, deposit details and rent records. Some buyers prefer a vacant house, so talk through timing first.

faqs.q: When are Oktibbeha County property taxes due?
faqs.a: February 1 for the previous assessment year. If that date lands on a weekend or holiday, paying the following Monday avoids any penalty.

faqs.q: Is a Starkville rental taxed differently from a home I live in?
faqs.a: Yes. Your own single-family home counts at 10 percent of true value, while a rental and other real property count at 15 percent.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Starkville?
faqs.a: At the shared Tax Assessor and Collector office, 101 East Main Street, or by calling 662-323-1273.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose problems when I sell in Mississippi?
faqs.a: Most sellers owe the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement before title transfers. A buyer who gets it late can cancel within three days of hand delivery or five days of mailing.
